Hook: On Capitol Hill in Washington, in the 1970s, about a hundred and fifty young couples ran a babysitting co-operative. Instead of paying each other in dollars, they paid in coupons, the co-op's own money: sit for another couple's children, and you earn coupons; go out for an evening, and you pay them. Couples liked to keep a reserve of coupons for the evenings they would need later. So, to build up their reserves, they stayed in and offered to sit. But if everyone wants to sit, nobody is going out, and nobody can earn anything. The co-op had a recession: a whole economy with willing workers, willing customers and nothing broken, except that hardly anyone was buying.

The Island has a co-op too, and Agora can run it. A hundred and fifty couples, each wanting 10 coupons in reserve. The dashed line is how many evenings out it could manage if everyone were happy with their reserve. It starts with only 4 coupons a couple, and it manages about 0.12 evenings a couple each week, barely half of what it could. In week 100, the board prints more coupons, up to 9 a couple. Evenings out rise to about 0.21. Nobody became more skilful or more willing. The co-op simply had too little money for what its members wanted to hold, and more money cured it.

In the 1930s the whole world asked the co-op's question. How can a whole economy be short of buyers? Why does output fall when no war or flood has destroyed the capacity to produce it? Why do prices and wages not simply fall until everyone who wants work has it? And what, if anything, can a government or a central bank do about it?
Economics, Built. Part twenty-seven: the Keynesian revolution.

Here is the plan. The Great Depression in the data, a choice for you, hoard or spend, and the co-op as a model of a whole economy. Then Keynes's answer: effective demand, the multiplier, and the paradox of thrift. The diagram that turned the book into a tool, the trap at zero interest, and a machine that ran the economy in coloured water. Why wages do not fall, and how demand and supply fit together. And what actually ended the Depression, Keynes's critics, two dials, the forecasting desk, and the newest twist: supply shocks that cut demand by more than themselves.
Depression: Chapter one. The Depression in data.

Start with what happened. Here is America's real output and its price level, each set to a hundred in 1929. From 1929 to 1933, real output fell by about 27 percent. Prices fell by about 26 percent. Falling prices are what the economics of the day said should cure a glut, and they did not. Output got back to its 1929 level only in 1937, and then fell again in the recession of 1937 and 1938.

And here is what it did to work: the unemployment rate, year by year, in one monthly series from the time. In 1929, about 1.4 percent by this series' count. In 1933, about 23 percent. Other estimates differ in the details, and put 1933 at about a quarter of the labour force. Either way, unemployment stayed in double digits for the rest of the decade, until the war.

What did economists expect? Jean-Baptiste Say had argued in 1803 that every sale is also a purchase: people produce in order to buy, so there can be no general glut of everything at once. Keynes later summed up the view in a phrase: supply creates its own demand. If workers are idle, wages fall until it pays to hire them. If goods go unsold, their prices fall until they sell. So a slump should cure itself, given time. The co-op shows the gap in the argument. A coupon earned by sitting need not be spent on an evening out. It can be held. When everyone wants to hold more money, the sale and the purchase come apart.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: hoard, or spend?

Your turn. You are a couple in the Island's co-op. You hold three coupons. You would like to have 10 in reserve before the busy season, when you know you will want to go out more. This week you could spend a coupon on an evening out, or stay in and offer to sit for someone else, to build up your reserve. Spend, or hoard? Pause, and choose.

There is no wrong answer for you alone. If you chose B, you were sensible: you are short of your reserve, and sitting is how you build it. But every couple in the co-op is short, so every couple chooses B. In Agora's co-op, each week about 26 percent of couples offer to sit, and only 12 percent go out. So an offer to sit finds a job only about 45 percent of the time, and nobody's reserve grows quickly, because the coupons are not there to be earned. What is wise for each couple is ruinous for the co-op as a whole. Economists call it the fallacy of composition, and it is the heart of this part.
Coop: Chapter three. The co-op as a model.

Here is the co-op as Agora runs it. Each couple wants 10 coupons in reserve. A couple at its reserve wants to go out in about 30 percent of weeks, and less often when it is short. Below its reserve, it is keen to sit; above it, less and less keen. An evening needs a couple going out and a couple sitting, so the number of evenings is set by the shorter queue. And the number of coupons in the co-op never changes, unless the board prints more. Notice what is not in the model: no couple is lazy, no sitter is unskilled, and nobody's taste for evenings out ever changes.

Now run the co-op with different amounts of money, from one coupon a couple to twenty-four, and watch a few years of weeks at each. In blue, the share of couples who want to go out each week. It rises with the coupons they hold. In violet, the share willing to sit. It falls as their reserves fill. In green, the evenings that actually happen: the shorter of the two queues. On the left, with too few coupons, everyone hoards and the co-op is in recession. More money raises output one for one with the willingness to spend. On the right, with too many coupons, nobody needs to sit, and evenings are scarce because sitters are: the co-op's version of an economy running too hot. In between, near 8 coupons a couple, it manages about 0.21 evenings a couple a week, as many as its members want. Output is set by demand on the left, and by capacity on the right.

Three lessons. First, a general glut is possible after all: when people want to hold more money than there is, they try to sell more than they buy, and everyone fails at once. Second, output can be set by spending, not by what the economy is able to produce. Third, the cure need not change anyone's character or skills. More money will do. The real co-op, by Krugman's account, first tried rules obliging members to go out, and recovered when more coupons were issued. One difference matters. The co-op fixed the price of an evening in coupons. In a real economy, prices and wages could fall, making each coupon worth more. Chapter nine asks why they fall so slowly.
Keynes: Chapter four. Keynes: effective demand and the multiplier.

In 1936 John Maynard Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. Its starting point is effective demand. Firms produce what they expect to sell, and hire the workers they need to produce it. So output, and with it employment, are set by planned spending, not by how many people want to work. The biggest part of spending is households' consumption, and Keynes proposed that it rises with income, but by less than income does. On the Island, consumption is two hundred plus 0.6 times income after taxes. That 0.6 is the marginal propensity to consume: the share of an extra dollar of income that is spent.

The Keynesian cross puts it in one picture. Planned spending is consumption, plus investment, plus the government's purchases. It rises with income, because consumption does. The dashed line is where spending equals income: what is bought equals what is produced. The economy settles where the two cross. On the Island, at an income of 1,600. If firms produced more, it would go unsold and they would cut back; if less, their shelves would empty and they would produce more. Solving, income is everything spent regardless of income, divided by one minus the propensity to consume. Now let the government buy 100 more. Income rises to 1,850: by 250, two and a half times the extra spending. That ratio is the multiplier.

Where does the multiplier come from? Follow the money. The government spends a hundred, on a bridge. That is a hundred of income for the builders. They spend 0.6 of it, sixty, in the shops: sixty more income for the shopkeepers. They spend thirty-six of that, and so on, each round smaller than the last. Add up the rounds and you get a geometric series: a hundred times one plus b plus b squared and so on, which is a hundred divided by one minus b. With b at 0.6, that is 250. Richard Kahn, Keynes's student, worked this out in 1931 for public works and jobs. Notice what makes it big: a high propensity to consume, and nothing else leaking out of the circle, into taxes, imports or higher interest rates. The next chapters add the leaks.
Thrift: Chapter five. The paradox of thrift.

Here is the co-op's lesson as arithmetic. Leave the government out, so that what households do not consume, they save. Saving rises with income, in violet. Investment, firms' spending on machines and buildings, is fixed at 300. The economy settles where saving equals investment, because only then is everything produced either consumed or invested: at an income of 1,250. Now every household decides to save 50 more, at any income. Income falls, to 1,125, by two and a half times the extra thrift, and total saving ends exactly where it began, at 300. Each household tried to save more; together they saved nothing more, and are poorer.

It can be worse. Suppose investment is not fixed, but rises with income, because firms build more when they sell more. Then thrift that cuts spending also cuts investment. Income falls from 1,667 to 1,500, and total saving falls too, from 467 to 450. An attempt to save more ends with less saved. It is called the paradox of thrift. Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees made a version of the point in 1714, and Keynes quoted it.

Be careful what this says. It holds when output is set by demand: when there are idle workers and idle machines, so that spending less means producing less. At full employment, the arithmetic changes. Saving frees resources for investment, and investment raises future income, which is the growth story of Part twenty. So thrift can be a vice in a slump and a virtue in a boom: the same act, in two different economies. After 2008, households paying down debts, firms hoarding cash and governments cutting deficits all tried to save at once, and the argument returned.
ISLM: Chapter six. I S, L M.

Keynes's book was long and hard. In 1937 John Hicks turned it into two curves, in a paper called Mister Keynes and the Classics. The first is the I S curve: every pair of income and interest rate at which spending equals output. It is the Keynesian cross, with one change: investment now falls when the interest rate rises. A higher rate means less investment, so less output: the curve slopes down. The second is the L M curve: every pair at which the money people want to hold equals the money there is. People want more money when their income is higher, for transactions, and less when the interest rate is higher, because holding money then costs more. So more income needs a higher interest rate to keep money demand equal to the fixed supply: the curve slopes up.

Draw them together, on the Island's numbers. The I S curve, sloping down. The L M curve, sloping up. They cross at an income of 1,446 and an interest rate of 2.5 percent. That is the one combination at which the goods market and the money market both clear. Nothing in it says that everyone who wants a job has one.

Now use it. Fiscal policy first: the government buys 50 more. The I S curve shifts right, and income rises to 1,523. But the multiplier is now only 1.54, not 2.5. Higher income raises the demand for money, the interest rate rises to 3.2 percent, and the higher rate crowds out some private investment. Monetary policy instead: the central bank adds 100 of money. The L M curve shifts right, the interest rate falls to 1.2 percent, and investment rises. Here it gives the same income, 1,523, by a different route. For thirty years this diagram was how economists, central banks and treasuries thought about a slump.
Trap: Now a slump. Firms lose confidence and investment collapses by 150 at every interest rate. The I S curve moves far to the left, and the economy settles at an income of 1,215, with the interest rate barely above zero. And the interest rate cannot go much below zero, because nobody lends at a negative rate when they could hold cash instead. Along that floor, the L M curve is flat. So the central bank prints. It adds 200 of money. The L M curve moves right, along the floor, and income rises to 1,225: almost nothing. People simply hold the extra money. That is Keynes's liquidity trap. Fiscal policy is another story. Spend 50 more, and income rises to 1,350: the full multiplier of 2.5, because the interest rate does not rise to crowd anything out.

For decades the trap looked like a curiosity of the 1930s. Then it came back. Japan's overnight interest rate was about 8 percent in 1990, as its bubble in land and shares burst. By 1996 it was below half a percent, and it stayed near zero for most of the next twenty-five years, while prices drifted down and growth stalled. America followed: after 2008, and again in 2020, the federal funds rate sat near zero, for 109 months in all.

In 1998, Paul Krugman wrote a paper about Japan called It's baaack, and asked what a central bank could do at zero. His answer starts from the real interest rate. Investment depends on the interest rate minus the inflation people expect. At a zero rate with prices expected to fall two percent a year, the real rate is two percent, and on the Island income falls further, to 1,100, compared with 1,225 with stable prices. If people instead expect prices to rise two percent, the real rate is minus two, and income rises to 1,350. So the central bank should promise to keep money easy even after the slump ends, and make people believe it. In Krugman's phrase, it must credibly promise to be irresponsible. The tools central banks used after 2008, forward guidance and large purchases of bonds, grew from that idea. Part thirty-one takes them up.
Machine: In 1949, a New Zealand engineer studying economics at the London School of Economics, Bill Phillips, built the Keynesian economy out of water. The first machine was built in a garage in Croydon. In it, income is water pumped to the top of the machine. It flows down through pipes and valves: some to consumption, some leaking away into saving, taxes and imports, while investment and government spending are pumped back in. About fourteen were built, for universities and central banks. Nine years later, the same Phillips drew the curve that bears his name, the subject of Part twenty-eight.

Agora can run a small version. The level of water in the tank is income. Each period, households spend 0.6 of what is left after taxes, which flows round again as someone else's income. Saving and taxes at 20 percent leak out. Investment and the government's purchases are pumped back in. The tank settles where the leaks exactly match what is pumped in: at 673. Now open the government's valve, 50 more each period. Watch the level climb, quickly at first, then more slowly, until it settles at 769. The multiplier is 1.92, smaller than the cross's two and a half, because taxes now leak too. And it takes time: the water has to go round.

What does a model made of water get right? That stocks and flows must add up: every dollar spent is someone's income, and nothing disappears. That adjustment takes time, and that the leaks set the size of the multiplier. And what does it leave out? Expectations: water does not anticipate that the valve will be opened next year, but people do, and Parts twenty-eight and twenty-nine show why that matters. And prices. In the machine, nothing gets cheaper when demand is short. In a real economy it does, slowly. That is the next question.
Wages: Chapter nine. Why wages do not fall.

The classical answer to a slump was that wages fall until it pays firms to hire everyone who wants work. Keynes had two objections. First, money wages are sticky. Workers resist cuts to their own pay, firm by firm, because a cut is a loss relative to other workers, even when everyone's pay would fall together. Second, and deeper: even if all wages did fall, firms' costs would fall, prices would follow, and real wages might not fall at all. A general cut in money wages is not a cut in real wages. And falling prices raise the real burden of debts that are fixed in money, which Irving Fisher called debt deflation, in 1933. That makes spending fall further.

Why are wages sticky? Truman Bewley went and asked. In 1992 and 1993, during a recession, he interviewed three hundred and thirty-six managers, union leaders and employment counsellors about how pay was set. Almost none had cut pay, even with many people looking for work who would have taken less. The reason they gave was morale. A pay cut feels like an insult, it makes workers less cooperative, and the best of them, who can find other jobs, leave first. So firms preferred to lay some people off and keep everyone else's pay, and the burden of the slump fell on the unemployed.

Here is what stickiness does to the data, on the Island. In blue, the pay changes firms would make if cuts were as easy as raises: an average rise of one percent, with 40 percent of workers due for a cut. Now suppose four in five of those cuts are not made, and the pay is frozen instead. In pink, what workers actually get: 32 percent get exactly zero, a spike, and only 8 percent are cut. Records of real pay show the same spike at zero, in study after study: David Card and Dean Hyslop's for America, and a project across sixteen countries led by William Dickens. When wages cannot fall far enough to clear the market, something else has to adjust, and that something is employment.
ASAD: Chapter ten. Aggregate demand and supply.

I S and L M hold prices fixed. To let them move, draw two new curves. Aggregate demand gives I S L M's output at each price level. A lower price level means more real money, a lower interest rate and more investment, so demand slopes down. But notice its bottom: below a price level of about three quarters, the interest rate is already at zero, and cheaper money buys nothing more. Demand turns vertical. In a trap, falling prices do not help. Aggregate supply: with money wages sticky, a higher price level lowers real wages, and firms hire and produce more. The dashed line is potential output, 1,450, where supply ends up once wages have had time to adjust. Today the curves cross very close to it.

Two kinds of shock. A demand shock first: the money supply falls by 100, as it did in America after 1929. Aggregate demand moves left. Output falls, from 1,448 to 1,417, and prices fall too, from 0.99 to 0.89: both down together, as in the 1930s. Now a supply shock instead: costs rise by fifteen percent, as when oil prices jumped in the 1970s. Aggregate supply moves up. Output falls by about as much, to 1,422, but prices rise, to 1.06. So the sign of the price change tells you which kind of shock hit. A demand slump brings deflation; a supply slump brings stagflation, and the policies that fight one make the other worse.

This picture became a peace treaty. In the short run, wages and prices are sticky, so Keynes is right: demand sets output, and policy can help. In the long run, wages adjust, output returns to its potential of 1,450, and only prices have changed: after the money shock, the price level ends near 0.83. The classics are right about the long run. So policy can shorten a slump, but it cannot raise what the economy can produce. Paul Samuelson called it the neoclassical synthesis, in his textbook from the 1955 edition, and it was the doctrine of a generation. Its weak point is the length of the short run. Keynes had written, in 1923, that the long run is a misleading guide to current affairs: in the long run we are all dead.
Ended: Chapter eleven. What ended the Depression?

What ended the Depression? The first answer is gold. Under the gold standard, every currency could be converted into gold at a fixed price. A central bank that was losing gold had to defend that price by raising interest rates and shrinking its money, in the middle of a slump. Britain left gold in September 1931. The United States left in 1933. France and the countries of the gold bloc held on until 1936. Barry Eichengreen and Jeffrey Sachs showed in 1985 that the earlier a country left gold, the sooner it recovered. In Eichengreen's phrase, gold was a set of golden fetters: it spread the Depression from country to country, and held each one in it.

The second answer is money, and in America the money came from gold. In March 1933, the country's gold stock was worth about 4 billion dollars. In January 1934, the government raised the price of gold from twenty dollars and sixty-seven cents an ounce to thirty-five, and the same gold was worth 7 billion. Then gold poured in, as Europe's savers fled the threat of war, to about 23 billion by 1941. The Treasury let it swell the money supply. In green, industrial production, rising with it, apart from the slump of 1937, when the Federal Reserve and the Treasury tightened. Christina Romer estimated in 1992 that nearly all of America's recovery before 1942 came from this monetary expansion, through lower real interest rates, and very little from fiscal policy, which was never large.

And then the war. American industrial production, which had been 8 in 1929 on today's index, reached about 17 at its wartime peak, more than double. Unemployment fell to the lowest rates on record. It was the biggest fiscal expansion in American history, paid for partly by borrowing from the banking system. Keynes's theory was tested by accident, at a scale no peacetime government would have tried. But the order of events matters. Output had already passed its 1929 level by 1937, before any war spending. Gold and money did the first part of the work; the war finished it.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the propensity to spend, and Okun's coefficient.

Two dials. The first returns from Part twenty-two, because the multiplier is built on it: how much of an extra dollar people spend. When the American government mailed tax rebates in 2001, with the week of each cheque set by the last digits of the taxpayer's Social Security number, households spent about thirty percent on nondurable goods within the quarter. The stimulus payments of 2008: about twenty percent on nondurables, and far more counting cars. The payments of 2020, when there was little to buy: about ten percent. Alaska's yearly oil dividend, in account data, about a quarter. Italians asked in a survey, about half. And the buffer-stock households of Part twenty-two, about a quarter within a year. These are shares of one-off windfalls in a quarter. The cross needs the share of a lasting rise in income spent over a year, which is larger, but once taxes and imports leak, the Island's six tenths is generous. Part thirty-two measures the multipliers themselves.

The second dial is new: Okun's coefficient, how many points unemployment rises for each point output falls below its potential. Arthur Okun, in 1962, found about three points of output for each point of unemployment: a coefficient of a third. Laurence Ball, Daniel Leigh and Prakash Loungani, fifty years on, found about minus point four five for the United States, and a fit that has hardly changed since 1948. But in Japan, where firms keep workers through slumps, about minus point one five. And in Spain, where temporary contracts are cut first, about minus point eight five. This film's own estimate, against the Congressional Budget Office's measures of potential output and the natural rate, is -0.62. It depends on the setting: on how a country's firms adjust, by hours, by hiring, or by firing.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: the forecasting desk.

Ninety years on, much of the work at a forecasting desk still starts from Keynes's accounting. Output is consumption plus investment plus government purchases plus net exports, so forecast each and add them up. Consumption from income, wealth and confidence; investment from firms' orders, interest rates and profits; the government's budget, with an assumption about its multipliers; and exports from the growth of trading partners. Then compare the total with what the economy could produce: the output gap, which tells the desk what to expect for unemployment and inflation.

Here are America's two gaps, quarter by quarter since 1949. In green, real output against the Congressional Budget Office's estimate of what the economy could produce. In pink, the unemployment rate against the Office's estimate of its natural rate, turned upside down so that bad times point down for both. They move together in every recession, the unemployment gap by a little more than half as much as output, and nowhere more sharply than in the spring of 2020.

That is one of the series' facts: Okun's law. In the data, the unemployment gap moves 0.62 points for each point of the output gap, and the line explains about 78 percent of the variation. The theory is this part's: when spending sets output, firms hire and lay off as their sales change, though not one for one, because hours, effort and productivity absorb some of it. So Agora fills in its column: about 1.6 points of output per point of unemployment in recent American data, against the three that Okun found, and the two the textbooks quote.

A second fact the desk lives with. Here is every American expansion and recession the National Bureau of Economic Research has dated, by the year it began. Since 1854 there have been 34 recessions. Expansions have lasted 41 months on average, recessions 17. Since 1945 the gap has widened: 64 months against 10. The longest expansion ran 128 months, from 2009 to the pandemic. Expansions are long and recessions short: the economy falls quickly and climbs slowly. Part twenty-nine asks what kind of model produces that.
